Lecture 18

Factors (from Lecture 16)

What are Factors?

  • Factors are variables in R which take on a limited number of different values, typically they are called non-numerical or “categorical” variables.
  • We use factors in statistical modeling because non-numerical variables (e.g., ancestry — African, Asian, European, Other) enter into statistical models differently than numerical variables.
  • Designating non-numerical data as factors insures that the modeling functions in R will treat these types of variables correctly.

Underneath a Factor

  • Factors in R are stored as a vector of integer values mapped to a corresponding set of character values. The character values are actually what gets displayed.
  • This is an efficient way to store character values, because each character value is stored only one time, and the data values are stored as a vector of integers. This requires far fewer computing resources.
  • This mechanism behind R’s factors and an AI’s chat window is the same: mapping human-readable text to machine-readable integers using a lookup dictionary.

Usefulness of factors

  • There exist cut() from base R and a variant in dplyr called ntile()
  • If you understand factors after today, you might find these two useful.
load("spotify_songs.RData")

## base R cut the values of variable into quartiles
pop_quartile <- cut(
      spotify_songs$track_popularity,
      breaks = quantile(spotify_songs$track_popularity, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.25)),
      include.lowest = TRUE
    )
is.factor(pop_quartile)
[1] TRUE
## base R cut the values according to custom breaks

pop_custom <- cut(
    spotify_songs$track_popularity,
    breaks = c(0, 25, 50, 75, 100),
    include.lowest = TRUE
)
is.factor(pop_custom)
[1] TRUE

visualized

  • Notice, we are not required to table the factor values in base R
old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE) # Save current settings
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(pop_quartile, main="result of quartile breaks", col = "blue")
plot(pop_custom, main = "result of cuts at custom values", col = "gold")
par(old_par) # Restore original settings

compare dplyr ntile()

  • ntile() is very exact, cut() can be sloppy and is better used if you do not need perfect balance
library(dplyr)
pop_ntile <- ntile(spotify_songs$track_popularity, 4) # forces balance
is(pop_ntile) # not a factor
[1] "integer"             "double"              "numeric"            
[4] "vector"              "data.frameRowLabels"
table(pop_ntile)
pop_ntile
   1    2    3    4 
8209 8208 8208 8208

visualized

barplot(table(pop_ntile), main = "result of ntile quarters", col = "cyan")

Understanding

  • Computers cannot do math on letters. So whether you are estimating a model in R in 101A or interacting with Claude/ChatGPT/etc., the system requires numbers to do its job.

  • In R (Factors): If you have a column of survey data with “Low,” “Medium,” and “High,” R assigns integers to represent the values (e.g., 1, 2, 3). It then attaches a dictionary called levels to remember that 1 means “Low.” This mapping allows statistical algorithms (like regression) to perform calculations on categories.

  • In AI (Tokenization): When you type a sentence into a chat window, the AI chops your words into chunks and assigns each chunk an ID number (e.g., “The” = 464, “cat” = 3432). It aslo uses a dictionary to remember what each number meant. This mapping allows the underlying models to perform linear algebra on your prompt.

  • In both cases, integers are used as placeholder for a string to save memory and enable complex math.

  • Of course they diverge tremendously: AI chunks words into fragments (e.g., “un” “remark” “able”) and the numeric values assigned to the fragments have no order. The dictionaries AI uses are also massive (e.g., 100,000 times larger than a factor’s levels in R)

Additional Info regarding factors

  • We can create factors using factor() BUT ALSO R can automatically designate variables as factors during certain types of data import or other forms of data reading.
  • Both numeric and character variables can be converted into factors, but a factor’s values (known as levels) will always be displayed as character values - for example numbers will have quotes around them because they are being displayed as character
  • So beware of numbers with quotes around them, it is a signal.

One issue from earlier in the course: Sorting and Ordering

Straight out of the documentation

Description

Sort (or order) a vector or factor (partially) into ascending or descending order. For ordering along more than one variable, e.g., for sorting data frames, see order.

sort() the values

Example

x <- c(8, 6, 7, 5, 3, 0, 9)
x
[1] 8 6 7 5 3 0 9

result of sort()

sort(x)
[1] 0 3 5 6 7 8 9

if you need to save the results, you will need to assign the sort to an object, below x is not sorted because we didn’t save it sorted, we can also demonstrate a decreasing sort and save it to y:

x
[1] 8 6 7 5 3 0 9
y <- sort(x, decreasing = TRUE)
y
[1] 9 8 7 6 5 3 0

Sorting Data Frames

This is not too useful on its own. What happens when we try to sort the data frame, don’t do this:

sort(iris)
Error in `xtfrm.data.frame()`:
! cannot xtfrm data frames

order() is used to sort (rearrange) data frames

The next statement sorts iris on the basis of Sepal.Length and saves the re-ordered result to a new data frame:

library(knitr)
iris2 <- iris[order(iris$Sepal.Length), ] 
head(iris2) |>  kable()

Complex sorting

If you want to get complex with a data frame sort, for example sort Petal.Width in increasing order and Sepal.Length in decreasing order within the values of the sorted Petal.Width. To do this, we will need to modify the method option to “radix”.

iris2 <- iris[order(iris$Petal.Width, iris$Sepal.Length, decreasing = c(FALSE,TRUE), method="radix"),]
kable(head(iris2))
Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species Sepal_Width_FACTOR Sepal_Width_to_numeric Sepal_Width_to_character_numeric

The apply family

Meet the apply() family

  • The apply family consists of vectorized functions which minimize your need to create (for) loops.

  • These functions will “apply” an R function or a set of R functions to an R data object.

  • We will examine the most common forms of apply functions used for data analysis but please understand that additional apply functions exist (mapply, rapply, and vapply) which will not be covered in Stats 20.

apply()

  • The apply() function is most often used to apply a function to the rows or columns (AKA the margins) of matrices or data frames.

  • Apply can be used with lists and arrays too. An array is a three-dimensional (r × c × h) object (imagine h stacked r × c matrices or a bunch of spreadsheets in an Excel document). All elements in an array must be of the same data type (character > numeric > logical). For example, Titanic is a built-in dataset

is.array(Titanic)
[1] TRUE
str(Titanic)

apply() syntax

The syntax for apply() is

apply(x, MARGIN, FUN, ...)

where…

  • x is the matrix, dataframe or array.

  • MARGIN is a vector giving the subscript(s) over which the function will be applied. For example, for a data frame or matrix 1 indicates rows, 2 indicates columns, c(1, 2) for both rows and columns. For an array, we can have higher order margins (e.g., 3, 4, etc.).

  • FUN is the function to be applied.

  • … is for any other arguments/options to be passed to the function, e.g., na.rm=TRUE

apply() and arrays

Recall the Titanic data set:

dimnames(Titanic)
$Class
[1] "1st"  "2nd"  "3rd"  "Crew"

$Sex
[1] "Male"   "Female"

$Age
[1] "Child" "Adult"

$Survived
[1] "No"  "Yes"
dim(Titanic)
[1] 4 2 2 2

Example - setup

Here is an example using a data frame, suppose I have a data frame of quiz scores for a small class, here are the first few rows:

apply(scores[, 2:4], 2, median)

dplyr (Tidyverse way)

  • It is useful to perform an apply() in dplyr because the philosophy is a little different, recall the fake data “scores”
  • In dplyr, to compute along the rows, you use rowwise() to change dplyer’s natural direction, then mutate() to create a new column, combined with any function and c_across().
  • The advantage is we are just augmenting our data frame with extra columns
library(dplyr)

scores %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(total_score = sum(c_across(q1:q3)), mean_score = mean(c_across(q1:q3))) %>%
  ungroup()
# A tibble: 10 × 6
     sid    q1    q2    q3 total_score mean_score

10    10    65    73    77         215       71.7
# Alternatively, you can use negative selection to say "sum everything EXCEPT..."
# scores %>%
# rowwise() %>%
#  mutate(total_score = sum(c_across(-sid)), mean(c_across(-sid, -total_score))) %>%
#  ungroup() # always ungroup

dplyr and columns

  • This is where dplyr is its happiest, it’s designed to work down columns.
  • Summarise will collapse the data frame to a single set of values
class_averages <- scores %>%
  summarise(across(q1:q3, mean))

class_stats <- scores %>%
  summarise(across(q1:q3, list(total = sum, average = mean, median = median, sd = sd)))

class_averages

  q3_total q3_average q3_median    q3_sd
1      778       77.8      77.5 3.966527

The question to ask when using dplyr working across rows or columns is: “am I creating a new variable (mutate) or collapsing my data down to a summary (summarise)?”.

lapply()

  • The lapply() function performs the following simple series of operations:
    • it loops over a list, iterating over each element in that list
    • it applies a function to each element of the list (a function that you specify)
    • it returns a list (the l in lapply stands for “list” or maybe “loop”).
  • The syntax for lapply() is as follows where
lapply(x, FUN, ...)
  • x is the list
  • FUN is the function to be applied
  • … is for any other arguments/option to be passed to the function (e.g., na.rm= TRUE)

lapply() and data frames

Interpretation of the result

  • We note that summary() doesn’t give us any usable statistics because R has stored the variables as character instead of numeric. This is caused by the commas, dollar and other characters in the data.

  • An easy way to remove the bad characters is to use an lapply() and write a small function to first remove the non-numeric characters and then convert the result to numeric. Further, this is only performed on columns 2 through 4:

budgetfixed <- data.frame(budgets$MovieTitle, 
                          lapply(budgets[,2:4], 
                                 function (x) as.numeric(gsub("[^[:digit:]\\.-]+","", x))))

lapply() with a (list) - webscraping application

  • lapply() with a generic vector (list), in this example, a collection of data frames scraped from Wikipedia. The steps involved below are:
    • use the rvest package to scrape a wikipedia page which has some (4) different tables with many rows
    • the page information is passed to a function in rvest which will extract the separate tables and store them in a list called “tables”
    • we will examine the first few tables in “tables”

The page

lapply() code

library(rvest)
wiki <- read_html("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_casual_dining_restaurant_chains")
tables <- wiki %>% html_nodes("table")  %>% html_table(fill=TRUE)
lapply(tables, dim)
[[1]]
[1] 322   5

[[2]]
[1] 219   5

[[3]]
[1] 8 5

[[4]]
[1] 54  5

[[5]]
[1] 14 12

[[6]]
[1] 2 2

[[7]]
[1] 5 8

[[8]]
[1] 3 2

[[9]]
[1] 12  2

Application

Suppose we want to know how many individual restaurants were listed on the web page. We could ask R to tell us how many rows (using the function nrow()) are in each table in the list named tables using an lapply:

lapply(tables[1:4], nrow) |> head()
[[1]]
[1] 322

[[2]]
[1] 219

[[3]]
[1] 8

[[4]]
[1] 54

We could convert the result of each nrow into a vector using unlist (the lapply result is a list, unlist converts to a vector) and use sum() to sum the vector values (assuming no duplicates). Using pipes, the lapply result is passed to unlist and that result is passed to sum.

lapply(tables[1:4], nrow) |>
    unlist() |>
    sum()
[1] 603

sapply()

The sapply() function behaves like lapply(); the only real difference is in the return value. sapply() will try to simplify (hence the “s”) the result of lapply() if possible. Essentially, sapply() calls lapply() on its input and then applies the following algorithm:

+ If the result is a list where every element is length 1, then a vector is returned
+ If the result is a list where every element is a vector of the same length (> 1), a matrix is returned.
+ If neither of the above simplifications can be performed then a list is returned

To illustrate the differences we can use the previous example using a list with restaurants and compare the sapply and lapply outputs:

sapply(tables[1:4], nrow)
[1] 322 219   8  54
sapply(tables[1:4], nrow) |>  sum()
[1] 603

Combining list components

  • In this example, the first 4 tables are lists of restaurants.
  • We can combine all 600+ into a single data frame, very easy in dplyr:
chainsD <- bind_rows(tables[1:4]) # dplyr
head(chainsD)
# A tibble: 6 × 6
  Name    Type  `Location(s)` `Number of locations` Notes Peak number of locat…¹
  <chr>   <chr> <chr>         <chr>                 <chr> <chr>                 
1 Adyar … Indi… India, Unite… 200+                  ""    <NA>                  
2 Americ… Pizza United State… 8                     ""    <NA>                  
3 Anchor… Amer… United State… 15                    ""    <NA>                  
4 Angus … Stea… United Kingd… 6                     ""    <NA>                  
5 Anjapp… Chet… Australia, C… 30+                   "Pri… <NA>                  
6 Annala… Indi… Australia, I… 4                     ""    <NA>                  
# ℹ abbreviated name: ¹​`Peak number of locations`

this is also do-able in base R, but it is less intuitive and much more fragile so it needs much more work

combined_df <- do.call(rbind, tables[1:4])
Error in `match.names()`:
! names do not match previous names

base R throws an error because the tables do not have the same columns.

tapply()

tapply() is used to apply a function over subsets of a vector. It is primarily used when we have the following circumstances: + A dataset that can be broken up into groups + Within each group, we want to apply a function to a numeric or logical value associated with the groups

The arguments to tapply() are as follows:

tapply(x, INDEX, FUN, ..., simplify = TRUE)
+ x is a numeric or logical vector
+ INDEX is a factor or a list of factors (or else they are coerced to factors) that identifies the groups
+ FUN is a function to be applied to each of the groups
+ ... contains optional arguments to be passed FUN
+ simplify, should we simplify the result? (TRUE/FALSE)

tapply() data

An example, we call up a built in dataset in dplyr called starwars:

kable(head(starwars[, 1:11]))
name height mass hair_color skin_color eye_color birth_year sex gender homeworld species
Luke Skywalker 172 77 blond fair blue 19.0 male masculine Tatooine Human
C-3PO 167 75 NA gold yellow 112.0 none masculine Tatooine Droid
R2-D2 96 32 NA white, blue red 33.0 none masculine Naboo Droid
Darth Vader 202 136 none white yellow 41.9 male masculine Tatooine Human
Leia Organa 150 49 brown light brown 19.0 female feminine Alderaan Human
Owen Lars 178 120 brown, grey light blue 52.0 male masculine Tatooine Human

tapply() example

Suppse we would like to know if the average (mean) mass of a character differs by species. We can use tapply() for this kind of analysis. Mass is measured for each character, we group each character by their species, we calculate the mean for each group, we pass the option na.rm = TRUE to insure that the function doesn’t return NA in the event of missing:

tapply(starwars$mass, starwars$species, mean, na.rm = TRUE)

group_by() in dplyr

dplyr has base R soundly beat here:

starwars %>% 
    group_by(species, gender) %>%
    summarise(observations = n(),
              mean.mass = mean(mass, na.rm = TRUE),
              sd.mass = sd(mass, na.rm = TRUE),
              median.height = median(height, na.rm = TRUE),
              iqr.height = IQR(height, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    arrange(desc(observations))
